Broadly speaking, I like to differentiate declarative macros based on access level.crate-exported: Intended to be exported from your crate and used by your dependentscrate-local: Intended to be used privately within your crateYou should prefer to keep macros crate-local if possible.Macros can be useful even if you don’t intend on exporting them. Actually, that’s most commonly how I make use of macros!The main way to differentiate between the two is whether a macro is marked with the #[macro_export] attribute. If not, then it’s a crate-local macro.

You should prefer to keep macros crate-local if possible.Macros can be useful even if you don’t intend on exporting them. Actually, that’s most commonly how I make use of macros!The main way to differentiate between the two is whether a macro is marked with the #[macro_export] attribute. If not, then it’s a crate-local macro.

Macros can be useful even if you don’t intend on exporting them. Actually, that’s most commonly how I make use of macros!The main way to differentiate between the two is whether a macro is marked with the #[macro_export] attribute. If not, then it’s a crate-local macro.

The main way to differentiate between the two is whether a macro is marked with the #[macro_export] attribute. If not, then it’s a crate-local macro.

For historic reasons, macros have two different ways they scope into the surrounding code.Textual Scoping: The macro scope is based on where in the file it’s definedPath-Based Scoping: The macro becomes an item in the module tree (acting more similarly to a standard Rust item)Where possible, you should prefer path-based scoping, but textual scoping can come in handy in some cases. Additionally, you’re very likely to run into heavy usage of the original textual scoping rules. So it’s worth understanding them regardless.

Where possible, you should prefer path-based scoping, but textual scoping can come in handy in some cases. Additionally, you’re very likely to run into heavy usage of the original textual scoping rules. So it’s worth understanding them regardless.

By default, declarative macros take on a textual scope.Textual scoped declarative macros have some counter-intuitive visibility and access rules.The macro may be used only after its definition within a module, function, or logical scope.The macro may be used by any submodules after the macro definition, even without importing it explicitly.So unlike other parts of the Rust language, order actually matters for textual scoped declarative macros.The most narrow visibility is within a logical scope (for example a function). Sometimes, though admittedly rarely, this can be useful for functions that have a lot of internal repetition.fn example() { macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } helper_macro!(); } // You cannot access this macro outside of the function. If the macro is going to be used in multiple items within the same module, you can simply define it in the module itself. This is more visible than within a single function, but it’s still constrained to only the current module and its submodules.// You cannot use it here, because it's not defined yet. macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } // Now it can be invoked and used. helper_macro!(); // It can be used within functions, as one might expect. fn within_functions() { helper_macro!(); } // Works within submodules of any depth as well, // which might feel counter-intuitive. mod even_within_submodules { helper_macro!(); } Sometimes it can be beneficial to use a macro from the parent module the containing module is defined under.Modern Rust syntax allows for this better with path-based scoping, which we’ll learn about in the next section.That said, you may still run into this syntax, so we should cover it.To hoist macros defined in a submodule into the parent’s textual scope, you can attach the #[macro_use] attribute on the containing module.// We still cannot use `helper_macro!` here, it isn't defined yet. // After the module definition completes, // it's now defined in the parent's textual scope. #[macro_use] mod submodule { macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } helper_macro!(); } // See? Now we can access and use it here even without an import. // It acts as-if we had defined it textually after `submodule`. helper_macro!(); // Works within submodules of any depth as well, // since it's a part of the textual scope. mod sibling_submodule { helper_macro!(); } But note that #[macro_use] will not automatically propagate further up the module tree.If you want your macro to continue to be defined all the way up the module tree, you’ll have to continue to attach the #[macro_use] attribute on all the parent modules.#[macro_use] // <- Necessary if you need it... mod outer_file { #[macro_use] mod other_file { macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } helper_macro!(); } helper_macro!(); } helper_macro!(); // <- ... at this location onwards. Historically, #[macro_use] was also used to import external macros from other crates into your textual scope.You should not be doing this anymore for macros imported from other crates, however.

This is more visible than within a single function, but it’s still constrained to only the current module and its submodules.// You cannot use it here, because it's not defined yet. macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } // Now it can be invoked and used. helper_macro!(); // It can be used within functions, as one might expect. fn within_functions() { helper_macro!(); } // Works within submodules of any depth as well, // which might feel counter-intuitive. mod even_within_submodules { helper_macro!(); } Sometimes it can be beneficial to use a macro from the parent module the containing module is defined under.Modern Rust syntax allows for this better with path-based scoping, which we’ll learn about in the next section.That said, you may still run into this syntax, so we should cover it.To hoist macros defined in a submodule into the parent’s textual scope, you can attach the #[macro_use] attribute on the containing module.// We still cannot use `helper_macro!` here, it isn't defined yet. // After the module definition completes, // it's now defined in the parent's textual scope. #[macro_use] mod submodule { macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } helper_macro!(); } // See? Now we can access and use it here even without an import. // It acts as-if we had defined it textually after `submodule`. helper_macro!(); // Works within submodules of any depth as well, // since it's a part of the textual scope. mod sibling_submodule { helper_macro!(); } But note that #[macro_use] will not automatically propagate further up the module tree.If you want your macro to continue to be defined all the way up the module tree, you’ll have to continue to attach the #[macro_use] attribute on all the parent modules.#[macro_use] // <- Necessary if you need it... mod outer_file { #[macro_use] mod other_file { macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } helper_macro!(); } helper_macro!(); } helper_macro!(); // <- ... at this location onwards. Historically, #[macro_use] was also used to import external macros from other crates into your textual scope.You should not be doing this anymore for macros imported from other crates, however.

You should not be doing this anymore for macros imported from other crates, however.

Path-based scoping for declarative macros allows us to work with macros in a way which feels more idiomatic.The macro works a lot like any other item, and can be invoked before the definition.In order to be used, it needs to be manually imported or resolved from the module tree.This can be accomplished with a small bit of code right after the macro definition:macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } // Re-export as an item in the module tree. pub(crate) use helper_macro; When you do this, since the macro is now a part of the module tree, order no longer matters.// Can call here, even if the macro isn't defined yet. helper_macro!(); macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } pub(crate) use helper_macro; // Can obviously still call here. helper_macro!(); Even though you can refer to macros out of order when they use path-based scoping, you’ll probably still want to define them before they’re used within the same file. Not because it’s necessary, but because it’s readable!The real benefit of this is that other modules can import and use the macro like they would any other item.mod submodule { macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } pub(crate) use helper_macro; } mod another_submodule { // You can use it like a normal item! use crate::submodule::helper_macro; helper_macro!(); // Or you can refer to it by a path! crate::submodule::helper_macro!(); } It’s most common to see this used with pub(crate), but you can really use all item visibilities here (pub(super), pub(in some::path), empty for private). pub has some strange properties, however - we’ll cover that in the next section.

It’s most common to see this used with pub(crate), but you can really use all item visibilities here (pub(super), pub(in some::path), empty for private). pub has some strange properties, however - we’ll cover that in the next section.

If you want a declarative macro to be usable from outside your crate, you have to attach the #[macro_export] attribute to it.Be careful when deciding to export a macro!After you export a macro, users may grow to depend on it, and it may become difficult to change or maintain. This is why I usually prefer not exporting a macro, until I’m sure it’s warranted.Still, if you’re sure it’s the right thing to do, you can accomplish it like so:#[macro_export] macro_rules! exported_macro { () => {}; } mod submodule { use crate::exported_macro; exported_macro!(); } The observable effects of this attribute are:The root of your crate will publicly export the macro for dependents to use (use your_crate::exported_macro).You can privately import the macro using normal path-based scoping (use crate::exported_macro).It doesn’t matter whether the macro is in a submodule or not, it will always export at the root.exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_export]` mod module { use crate::exported_macro; exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of the `use` statement mod submodule { #[macro_export] macro_rules! exported_macro { () => {}; } } exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of the `use` statement } exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_export]` The #[macro_use] attribute still has an effect privately within your crate, as one would expect for textual scoping rules. Though, I don’t recommend using it on modules containing exported macros, instead just go through the exported path.exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_export]` mod module { // <- Would not be usable here without a `use` statement #[macro_use] mod submodule { #[macro_export] macro_rules! exported_macro { () => {}; } } exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_use]` } exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_export]` If you want to export a macro somewhere other than the crate root, there’s a way to allow for that.It would be nice if you could just not use #[macro_export], and instead pub use exported_macro, but as for now this doesn’t work. If you try it, you will be met with a compile error that the macro is “only public within the crate, and cannot be re-exported”.So, you MUST use #[macro_export] on exported macros. Then, you can bind that exported macro to a specific location in the module tree with pub use exported_macro.That’s annoying since it’ll publish a macro in the root (which you probably don’t intend), so the general pattern for this is:Hide the publicly exported macro (so folks can’t see it’s actually at the root).Create a public path binding in the module where you want the macro to be accessed from.So, for instance:pub mod submodule { // Since this is `#[macro_export]`, // it will still wind up at the crate root. // // Because of that, we name this in a way that deters usage. // We'll also hide it, so that it doesn't appear in docs. #[doc(hidden)] #[macro_export] macro_rules! __exported_macro { () => {}; } /// The actual documentation will go here! #[doc(inline)] pub use __exported_macro as exported_macro; } // Technically this does export the following macro... crate::__exported_macro!(); // However, documentation will only list this version. // And, this version will be public for dependents to use. crate::submodule::exported_macro!(); In future versions of Rust, this cruft around visibility and module tree exporting may get cleaned up.It’s hard to make changes like this to the Rust language that won’t break existing code. So this has remained one of those weird parts of the language which - if you’re not careful - can work in odd, non-idiomatic ways.There’s a pretty in-depth thread about this here on the Rust internals forum.

Then, you can bind that exported macro to a specific location in the module tree with pub use exported_macro.That’s annoying since it’ll publish a macro in the root (which you probably don’t intend), so the general pattern for this is:Hide the publicly exported macro (so folks can’t see it’s actually at the root).Create a public path binding in the module where you want the macro to be accessed from.So, for instance:pub mod submodule { // Since this is `#[macro_export]`, // it will still wind up at the crate root. // // Because of that, we name this in a way that deters usage. // We'll also hide it, so that it doesn't appear in docs. #[doc(hidden)] #[macro_export] macro_rules! __exported_macro { () => {}; } /// The actual documentation will go here! #[doc(inline)] pub use __exported_macro as exported_macro; } // Technically this does export the following macro... crate::__exported_macro!(); // However, documentation will only list this version. // And, this version will be public for dependents to use. crate::submodule::exported_macro!(); In future versions of Rust, this cruft around visibility and module tree exporting may get cleaned up.It’s hard to make changes like this to the Rust language that won’t break existing code. Recall from our prior article, when we talked about macro hygiene, that Rust uses what’s known as “mixed-site hygiene”.Most items - other than local variables - are resolved from where the macro is invoked (functions, types, traits, etc.). For crate-local macros, you can be a little looser with this and require that the invoking code imports some items as needed to compile. But for crate-exported macros, it’s not a good idea to force the user to do this.Because of that, you should keep the following things in mind:You usually want to avoid using the crate keyword directly, because it may not refer to your crate.Since you’re in less control over the surrounding code for crate-exported macros, you should not assume anything about what has been imported at the invocation site.For declarative macros, there’s a special, always-present meta-variable called $crate, which resolves to the crate that your declarative macro is defined in. So it’s usually prudent to use that as a common reference point for any items needed by your macro’s expansion.// Example type - pretend we have a full type definition. pub struct MyCustomHashMap { /*...*/ } /// A declarative macro that produces a hash map. /// /// Note: Actually, the standard is attempting to add this! /// See: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.hash_map.html #[macro_export] macro_rules! hash_map { ( $( $key:expr => $value:expr ),* $(,)? ) => {{ // Use our hashmap implementation from our crate. let mut map = $crate::MyCustomHashMap::new(); $( map.insert($key, $value); )* map }} } #[test] fn example() { let map = hash_map! { "key" => "value", }; assert_eq!(map.get("key"), Some(&"value")); } In the above example we demonstrate this with a MyCustomHashMap which our crate also exports. Other standing functions, or other required traits, would also need to be resolved via $crate.If your macro depends on items from other crates, it’s often wise to re-export those dependencies in a public module hidden within your crate. We usually name this something like __private and mark it #[doc(hidden)] to deter usage.#[doc(hidden)] pub mod __private { // Publicly re-export things that your macro uses here. } The serde crate does this with its own __private module. Though, their instance of it may be more for their procedural macros (Serialize and Deserialize). After all, this isn’t a problem specific to declarative macros.

Macros very often don’t have a specific type they’re bound to, usually they’re general convenience macros.That being the case, I recommend the following organization strategy:For macros which are constrained to a single module or function, just define them where they’re needed.For macros which are shared across multiple modules, define them in a common parent module.Tip: For smaller crates, this can often be easiest to target the top-most module (lib.rs).I don’t like to carelessly slap macros into some parent module (or I have several of them, which becomes unwieldy). So I put them in separate files for each macro that I define, and then re-export them into some organizational parent module.Crate-exported macros fit into this pretty well. In those cases, I just don’t re-export into the parent if the intended way to access the macro is by from the crate root.This harkens back to my module organization article, where I detail methods of using “organizational modules”, and defining types in their own separate files.Please take a look at that if you are having trouble understanding my organization strategy.mod.rs: (organizational module; often lib.rs)mod macros; mod type_a; mod type_b; mod type_c; // etc... macros/mod.rs: (organizational module)// Modules: mod exported_macro; mod helper_macro_a; mod helper_macro_b; mod helper_macro_c; // etc... // Re-Exports: pub(crate) use helper_macro_a::*; pub(crate) use helper_macro_b::*; pub(crate) use helper_macro_c::*; // etc... macros/exported_macro.rs:// In this case, I'm happy to bind it to the root. #[macro_export] macro_rules! exported_macro { () => {}; } macros/helper_macro_a.rs:macro_rules! helper_macro_a { () => {}; } pub(crate) use helper_macro_a; Elsewhere in the crate:// Either pull them in for usage: use crate::macros::{helper_macro_a, helper_macro_b}; helper_macro_a!(); helper_macro_b!(); // Or refer to them via absolute paths: crate::macros::helper_macro_c!(); I know this seems like overkill, but the nice thing about this is I can always very easily find a macro. Either the macro is defined near its usage (so it’s within the same file), or the file is named the same thing as the macro so it’s easy to open via a command.If a macro is very closely related to another macro, and they’re only split up for ease of maintenance, I usually put them in the same file. But I only do that if they are meant to be implementation details of the main macro intended to be invoked.And, you don’t always need an organizing macros module - you could just re-export the macros right into the main organizational module. That’s for each person and project to decide on.

I don’t like to carelessly slap macros into some parent module (or I have several of them, which becomes unwieldy). So I put them in separate files for each macro that I define, and then re-export them into some organizational parent module.Crate-exported macros fit into this pretty well. In those cases, I just don’t re-export into the parent if the intended way to access the macro is by from the crate root.This harkens back to my module organization article, where I detail methods of using “organizational modules”, and defining types in their own separate files.Please take a look at that if you are having trouble understanding my organization strategy.mod.rs: (organizational module; often lib.rs)mod macros; mod type_a; mod type_b; mod type_c; // etc... macros/mod.rs: (organizational module)// Modules: mod exported_macro; mod helper_macro_a; mod helper_macro_b; mod helper_macro_c; // etc... // Re-Exports: pub(crate) use helper_macro_a::*; pub(crate) use helper_macro_b::*; pub(crate) use helper_macro_c::*; // etc... macros/exported_macro.rs:// In this case, I'm happy to bind it to the root. #[macro_export] macro_rules! exported_macro { () => {}; } macros/helper_macro_a.rs:macro_rules! helper_macro_a { () => {}; } pub(crate) use helper_macro_a; Elsewhere in the crate:// Either pull them in for usage: use crate::macros::{helper_macro_a, helper_macro_b}; helper_macro_a!(); helper_macro_b!(); // Or refer to them via absolute paths: crate::macros::helper_macro_c!(); I know this seems like overkill, but the nice thing about this is I can always very easily find a macro. Either the macro is defined near its usage (so it’s within the same file), or the file is named the same thing as the macro so it’s easy to open via a command.If a macro is very closely related to another macro, and they’re only split up for ease of maintenance, I usually put them in the same file. But I only do that if they are meant to be implementation details of the main macro intended to be invoked.And, you don’t always need an organizing macros module - you could just re-export the macros right into the main organizational module. That’s for each person and project to decide on.

Now that we know how to integrate declarative macros into our project, let’s look at some use cases for them.At the risk of sounding like a broken record - I would like to remind you to try as hard as possible NOT to export the macro.A crate-local macro, as stated, is really nice because users only depend on the side effects of it. You control the syntax and the places it’s invoked completely. There’s less to worry about with respects to breaking changes, or dependencies on unintended usage of the macro.Only export a macro if you’re sure it’s a wise decision.

You control the syntax and the places it’s invoked completely. There’s less to worry about with respects to breaking changes, or dependencies on unintended usage of the macro.Only export a macro if you’re sure it’s a wise decision.

There’s less to worry about with respects to breaking changes, or dependencies on unintended usage of the macro.Only export a macro if you’re sure it’s a wise decision.

Only export a macro if you’re sure it’s a wise decision.

While developing a crate, you may author types that have some nearly-identically-implemented functions or traits.If the types are semantically closely related, we can reduce duplication using a helper macro. The helper macro will implement the common traits or function, with some information provided to it.Some specific examples of when this is beneficial include:If you need to author several types which are mostly simple wrappers of other types (something like a newtype).If you want to ensure several types have an identical subset of an API (functions and traits).Be careful not to reach for declarative macros at the smallest sign of duplication, though. Instead, you should consider it when things appear to be very cut-and-paste. If you over-generalize, that could make maintenance more of a burden, not less.For implementation macros like these, I like to follow a key = value pattern.macro_rules! impl_example { ( input_1 = $input_1:literal, input_2 = ($($input_2:tt)*), input_3 = { grouped_input_1 = $grouped_input_1:literal, grouped_input_2 = $grouped_input_2:ident, grouped_input_3 = $grouped_input_3:expr, }, input_4 = [$($input_4:expr),* $(,)?], ) => { /*Expansion Here*/ }; } impl_example! { input_1 = 123, input_2 = (complex; grouped, input), input_3 = { grouped_input_1 = "sample", grouped_input_2 = Sample, grouped_input_3 = concat!("..."), // ... }, input_4 = [ array_value_1, array_value_2, array_value_3, // ... ], // ... etc ... } My reason for preferring this syntax is:You cannot accidentally map a fragment to the wrong input without it being visible at the call site.It uses a different binding syntax from struct initialization to distance itself from appearing to initialize an object.Despite the binding syntax being different, it feels familiar enough to be immediately understood.Though, I’ll admit the last two points aren’t that important. If you feel more comfortable you could use a more “struct field initialization” style format (key: value). That’s up to you!Don’t over-generalize these, accept them in one order - we’re only using these internally after all.I sometimes like to order them alphanumerically by key name, so that the order is at least consistent.ExamplesAn example of this in the wild are the integer types in the Rust language itself. Integer types (like u8) use a crate-local int_impl macro to implement common functions and traits.It’s also common to use declarative macros to assist in implementing a trait across tuples of different arities. Commonly useful in cases where your trait will just call the same trait on all tuple elements. You can see an example of this in the serde crate with the crate-local tuple_impls! macro.If you’d like a toy example - here’s one using some strongly typed time values. The macro helps us ensure the conversion implementations are consistent between the different types.#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub struct OverflowError; #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Hours(u32); #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Minutes(u32); #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Seconds(u32); macro_rules! impl_time_functionality { ( from = [$($from:ty),* $(,)?], seconds_per = $seconds_per:expr, try_from = [$($try_from:ty),* $(,)?], type = $type:ty, ) => { // Ensure that we have common functions that we expect all of these time types to have. // // Reminder that you can open multiple impl blocks for a single type, so if there are // functions that don't make sense to be commonly implemented here, then just write them // in a separate impl block for the intended type outside of this macro. impl $type { // Helper constant to facilitate conversion impls. // We don't want to export it publicly from this case. pub(crate) const SECONDS_PER: u32 = $seconds_per; pub fn to_u32(self) -> u32 { self.0 } } $( impl TryFrom<$try_from> for $type { type Error = OverflowError; fn try_from(value: $try_from) -> Result { // This const assert ensures we haven't used the helper macro improperly. const _: () = assert!( <$try_from>::SECONDS_PER > $seconds_per, concat!(stringify!($try_from), " must contain more seconds than ", stringify!($type)), ); Ok(Self(value.to_u32() .checked_mul(<$try_from>::SECONDS_PER / Self::SECONDS_PER) .ok_or(OverflowError)?)) } } )* $( impl From<$from> for $type { fn from(value: $from) -> Self { // This const assert ensures we haven't used the helper macro improperly. const _: () = assert!( <$from>::SECONDS_PER < $seconds_per, concat!(stringify!($from), " must contain fewer seconds than ", stringify!($type)), ); Self(value.to_u32() / (Self::SECONDS_PER / <$from>::SECONDS_PER)) } } )* }; } impl_time_functionality! { from = [], seconds_per = 1, try_from = [ Minutes, Hours ], type = Seconds, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds ], seconds_per = 60, try_from = [ Hours ], type = Minutes, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds, Minutes ], seconds_per = 60 * 60, try_from = [], type = Hours, } #[test] fn test() { assert_eq!(Hours::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Seconds(60 * 60)); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Minutes(60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Minutes(60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Minutes(60)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Hours(1)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Minutes(60))); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); } Sometimes the deduplication is not worth the obfuscation that it creates, but that’s a case-by-case thing. For simple types like this (and the integer types from the standard library), the benefit is clear, as it produces the obvious intended end result and ensures the APIs are all implemented uniformly.If you find yourself adding a lot of special-casing and splitting your macro into many separate macros, that might be a sign that you’ve attempted to use this pattern in a place where it’s not helpful.In those cases, it’s probably best to just write out all your traits and impls by-hand, even if it results in some duplication.

{ from = [], seconds_per = 1, try_from = [ Minutes, Hours ], type = Seconds, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds ], seconds_per = 60, try_from = [ Hours ], type = Minutes, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds, Minutes ], seconds_per = 60 * 60, try_from = [], type = Hours, } #[test] fn test() { assert_eq!(Hours::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Seconds(60 * 60)); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Minutes(60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Minutes(60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Minutes(60)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Hours(1)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Minutes(60))); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); } Sometimes the deduplication is not worth the obfuscation that it creates, but that’s a case-by-case thing. For simple types like this (and the integer types from the standard library), the benefit is clear, as it produces the obvious intended end result and ensures the APIs are all implemented uniformly.If you find yourself adding a lot of special-casing and splitting your macro into many separate macros, that might be a sign that you’ve attempted to use this pattern in a place where it’s not helpful.In those cases, it’s probably best to just write out all your traits and impls by-hand, even if it results in some duplication.

Be careful not to reach for declarative macros at the smallest sign of duplication, though. Instead, you should consider it when things appear to be very cut-and-paste. If you over-generalize, that could make maintenance more of a burden, not less.For implementation macros like these, I like to follow a key = value pattern.macro_rules! impl_example { ( input_1 = $input_1:literal, input_2 = ($($input_2:tt)*), input_3 = { grouped_input_1 = $grouped_input_1:literal, grouped_input_2 = $grouped_input_2:ident, grouped_input_3 = $grouped_input_3:expr, }, input_4 = [$($input_4:expr),* $(,)?], ) => { /*Expansion Here*/ }; } impl_example! { input_1 = 123, input_2 = (complex; grouped, input), input_3 = { grouped_input_1 = "sample", grouped_input_2 = Sample, grouped_input_3 = concat!("..."), // ... }, input_4 = [ array_value_1, array_value_2, array_value_3, // ... ], // ... etc ... } My reason for preferring this syntax is:You cannot accidentally map a fragment to the wrong input without it being visible at the call site.It uses a different binding syntax from struct initialization to distance itself from appearing to initialize an object.Despite the binding syntax being different, it feels familiar enough to be immediately understood.Though, I’ll admit the last two points aren’t that important. If you feel more comfortable you could use a more “struct field initialization” style format (key: value). That’s up to you!Don’t over-generalize these, accept them in one order - we’re only using these internally after all.I sometimes like to order them alphanumerically by key name, so that the order is at least consistent.ExamplesAn example of this in the wild are the integer types in the Rust language itself. Integer types (like u8) use a crate-local int_impl macro to implement common functions and traits.It’s also common to use declarative macros to assist in implementing a trait across tuples of different arities. The macro helps us ensure the conversion implementations are consistent between the different types.#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub struct OverflowError; #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Hours(u32); #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Minutes(u32); #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Seconds(u32); macro_rules! impl_time_functionality { ( from = [$($from:ty),* $(,)?], seconds_per = $seconds_per:expr, try_from = [$($try_from:ty),* $(,)?], type = $type:ty, ) => { // Ensure that we have common functions that we expect all of these time types to have. // // Reminder that you can open multiple impl blocks for a single type, so if there are // functions that don't make sense to be commonly implemented here, then just write them // in a separate impl block for the intended type outside of this macro. impl $type { // Helper constant to facilitate conversion impls. // We don't want to export it publicly from this case. pub(crate) const SECONDS_PER: u32 = $seconds_per; pub fn to_u32(self) -> u32 { self.0 } } $( impl TryFrom<$try_from> for $type { type Error = OverflowError; fn try_from(value: $try_from) -> Result { // This const assert ensures we haven't used the helper macro improperly. const _: () = assert!( <$try_from>::SECONDS_PER > $seconds_per, concat!(stringify!($try_from), " must contain more seconds than ", stringify!($type)), ); Ok(Self(value.to_u32() .checked_mul(<$try_from>::SECONDS_PER / Self::SECONDS_PER) .ok_or(OverflowError)?)) } } )* $( impl From<$from> for $type { fn from(value: $from) -> Self { // This const assert ensures we haven't used the helper macro improperly. const _: () = assert!( <$from>::SECONDS_PER < $seconds_per, concat!(stringify!($from), " must contain fewer seconds than ", stringify!($type)), ); Self(value.to_u32() / (Self::SECONDS_PER / <$from>::SECONDS_PER)) } } )* }; } impl_time_functionality! { from = [], seconds_per = 1, try_from = [ Minutes, Hours ], type = Seconds, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds ], seconds_per = 60, try_from = [ Hours ], type = Minutes, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds, Minutes ], seconds_per = 60 * 60, try_from = [], type = Hours, } #[test] fn test() { assert_eq!(Hours::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Seconds(60 * 60)); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Minutes(60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Minutes(60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Minutes(60)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Hours(1)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Minutes(60))); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); } Sometimes the deduplication is not worth the obfuscation that it creates, but that’s a case-by-case thing. For simple types like this (and the integer types from the standard library), the benefit is clear, as it produces the obvious intended end result and ensures the APIs are all implemented uniformly.If you find yourself adding a lot of special-casing and splitting your macro into many separate macros, that might be a sign that you’ve attempted to use this pattern in a place where it’s not helpful.In those cases, it’s probably best to just write out all your traits and impls by-hand, even if it results in some duplication.

It’s also common to use declarative macros to assist in implementing a trait across tuples of different arities. A really popular use for declarative macros is to wrap the format! macro from the standard library, adapting the formatting syntax for another related use-case.// Because we assume the user will call `some_adapter` a lot. // To make this easier on them, we have a small helper macro. // // Instead of a plain function, where the user types: // some_adapter(format!(...)) // // They can import this macro and type: // some_adapter!(...) #[macro_export] macro_rules! some_adapter { ($($msg:tt)*) => { $crate::__private::some_adapter(format!($($msg)*)) } } You don’t always need to provide such a macro, sometimes you can just take impl Into and let the user format as they please. But it can make things more readable in cases where the user will always be formatting a string, or if you want formatting to be conditionally compiled-out when disabling alloc support.ExamplesTo point at the standard library again, we can look at the todo! macro. It’s simple enough that it’s just implemented right there as a declarative macro instead of being a built-in like many other macros (similar to assert_eq!, matches!, and a few others).It’s a bit of a low-hanging fruit, but the log crate has some pretty obvious examples; info!, warn!, and error!. In general, anything with a format!-like operation benefits from a declarative macro.assert!-like macros are another example of this kind of macro. You may not think too much about it, but it can be nice to provide added details about a failure for unit tests. The assert! macros all accept format arguments at the end, and you can too if you need some adapter assert! macro.macro_rules! assert_in_range { ($input:expr, $low:expr, $high:expr, $($msg:tt)*) => {{ let input = $input; let low = $low; let high = $high; assert!( input >= $low, "{}: range check failed: {input} >= {low}", format_args!($($msg)*), ); assert!( input <= $high, "{}: range check failed: {input} <= {high}", format_args!($($msg)*), ); }}; } #[test] fn example() { let number = 5; assert_in_range!(number, 50, 100, "formatted example (input={})", number); } The failure here looks like this:thread 'example' (50) panicked at src/lib.rs:22:5: formatted example (input=5): range check failed: 5 >= 50 note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace

For many types, you can get away with either the struct initialization format, or using the builder pattern.#[derive(Default)] struct Example { foo: u8, bar: String, baz: bool, } // Some initialization patterns: fn struct_initialization() { let object = Example { foo: 0, bar: format!("example formatted string"), baz: false, }; } fn struct_initialization_partial() { let object = Example { bar: format!("example formatted string"), ..Example::default() }; } fn builder_pattern() { // `ExampleBuilder` type not shown for brevity. let object = ExampleBuilder::default() .with_foo(123) .with_bar(format!("example formatted string")) .finish(); } But sometimes we want a different syntax than this, for readability reasons.Often custom syntaxes are only beneficial if there’s some common, well-accepted, pre-existing format (e.g. an existing data markup language, like JSON). But occasionally a purely custom syntax can be helpful.Containers are a great example of custom initialization syntax that everyone should have some experience with.It’s true you can (and should) implement FromIterator to initialize from some sequence of elements. But this syntax can be awkward for explicit initialization that isn’t coming from some already constructed values. So for developer convenience we often create small helper macros to improve readability.Like with many things relating to macros, only add them when you’re sure they’re useful. Think about whether the pre-existing methods for initializing objects is good enough.ExamplesIt should go without saying, but the vec! macro is a really popular example of this. And soon we will have yet another version of this, with the hash_map! macro.The best example of this I can think of for object initialization is the json! macro from the serde_json crate.This is actually a good example of using declarative macros to do something non-trivial. Specifically, note that they hide the implementation details of the macro by splitting it into multiple macros, json! is the main one you call, and it redirects to another exported macro which is hidden from documentation called json_internal.Though, I will admit, json! is one of those declarative macros I think is teetering on the edge of “should have been a procedural macro”. Though, it might be hard to safely change it over at this point.

ExamplesIt should go without saying, but the vec! macro is a really popular example of this. And soon we will have yet another version of this, with the hash_map! macro.The best example of this I can think of for object initialization is the json! macro from the serde_json crate.This is actually a good example of using declarative macros to do something non-trivial. Specifically, note that they hide the implementation details of the macro by splitting it into multiple macros, json! is the main one you call, and it redirects to another exported macro which is hidden from documentation called json_internal.Though, I will admit, json! is one of those declarative macros I think is teetering on the edge of “should have been a procedural macro”. Though, it might be hard to safely change it over at this point.

Though, I will admit, json! is one of those declarative macros I think is teetering on the edge of “should have been a procedural macro”. Though, it might be hard to safely change it over at this point.

Sometimes you find yourself writing many similar lines of code within a small set of functions.In most cases, it’s best to just change these into helper functions and let the compiler optimize things. But sometimes you’ll run into situations where you can’t do that.You need to generate a distinct type per functional configuration (e.g. not just logic or impls).You’re using it to provide the body of a function that the macro is implementing, and you can’t generalize this function body over any trait bounds.When your macro influences the surrounding control flow (break, continue, return).For optimization reasons (which you have surely bench tested).Be careful when altering control flow.It can have some utility for really simple, localized helper macros. But I tend to consider it to be an anti-pattern to export such macros. However, used very sparingly, in unique cases to assist in implementing something, it can be helpful.Honestly, I even lean away from it for crate-local macros as well. Obfuscating the control flow negatively impacts readability in my experience.ExamplesOne example where this pattern being used for optimization reasons is within the Rust standard library. The str type specializes based on string lengths for optimization reasons (specialize_for_lengths; used here).The bytes crate actually uses some macros to reduce code duplication. See the crate-local buf_get_impl macro. This is a good example of the macro providing a common implementation for a set functions. The functions that are being implemented simply invoke the macro to expand this common implementation.An example of a crate-exported macro used to produce new types can be found in the bitflags crate. In this case, it uses some custom syntax that looks kind of like regular Rust code, so it’s a good reference for how to use some different fragment specifiers (like meta or vis).Finally, probably one of the most popular control-flow-impacting macros, is anyhow’s bail! macro. As mentioned, I’m not a fan of these kinds of macros (including this one). But I want to mention it anyway, since it fits within this set of example use-cases, and likely has some popularity. (Another potential example of this is the standard library’s ready! macro for polling futures.)A really simple example of this is constructing a newtype that redirects to the underlying implementation. We may want to ensure that the types are actually distinct from one another, but we may not want to re-implement the functionality the type provides (impl_displayable_type - example usage here - is an example of this from one of my own crates, typed-ident).// A simplified form of `impl_displayable_type` to use as an example. macro_rules! impl_displayable_type { ( name=$name:ident, over=$over:ident, docs=$docs:expr, ) => { #[doc = $docs] pub struct $name($over); impl core::fmt::Display for $name { #[inline] fn fmt(&self, f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> core::fmt::Result { self.0.fmt(f) } } }; } // We have some displayable types that we don't want to conflate. impl_displayable_type! { name = ObjectId, over = u64, docs = "Example documentation here", } impl_displayable_type! { name = GroupId, over = u64, docs = concat!( "`docs` is an expression so you can do things like this.\n", "\n", "Multi-line documentation, for better readability!", ), } // So now, if we have an API like this... struct Object; impl Object { pub fn object_id(&self) -> ObjectId { todo!() } pub fn group_id(&self) -> GroupId { todo!() } } // ... You can't accidentally do something like this. fn example_bad_usage_that_no_longer_compiles(object: Object) { let group_id: GroupId = object.object_id(); // Fails to compile! } It can be tempting to use declarative macros in places where a #[derive(...)] procedural macro would make more sense. Try to avoid creating such macros unless necessary.A common toy example for declarative macros is to create a function on enums so you can get static strings of the enum variant names. But this can be accomplished through a derive macro, and that feels more idiomatic to me (like IntoStaticStr from the strum crate, or - maybe better - having a custom trait to represent this).Do what you believe the end-user would find most natural. If what your macro is doing is implementing a trait - you probably ought to make it a derive macro unless you have good reason not to.We’ll talk more about derive macros when we cover procedural macros in a later article, though.

(Another potential example of this is the standard library’s ready! macro for polling futures.)A really simple example of this is constructing a newtype that redirects to the underlying implementation. We may want to ensure that the types are actually distinct from one another, but we may not want to re-implement the functionality the type provides (impl_displayable_type - example usage here - is an example of this from one of my own crates, typed-ident).// A simplified form of `impl_displayable_type` to use as an example. macro_rules! impl_displayable_type { ( name=$name:ident, over=$over:ident, docs=$docs:expr, ) => { #[doc = $docs] pub struct $name($over); impl core::fmt::Display for $name { #[inline] fn fmt(&self, f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> core::fmt::Result { self.0.fmt(f) } } }; } // We have some displayable types that we don't want to conflate. impl_displayable_type! { name = ObjectId, over = u64, docs = "Example documentation here", } impl_displayable_type! { name = GroupId, over = u64, docs = concat!( "`docs` is an expression so you can do things like this.\n", "\n", "Multi-line documentation, for better readability!", ), } // So now, if we have an API like this... struct Object; impl Object { pub fn object_id(&self) -> ObjectId { todo!() } pub fn group_id(&self) -> GroupId { todo!() } } // ... You can't accidentally do something like this. fn example_bad_usage_that_no_longer_compiles(object: Object) { let group_id: GroupId = object.object_id(); // Fails to compile! } It can be tempting to use declarative macros in places where a #[derive(...)] procedural macro would make more sense. Try to avoid creating such macros unless necessary.A common toy example for declarative macros is to create a function on enums so you can get static strings of the enum variant names. But this can be accomplished through a derive macro, and that feels more idiomatic to me (like IntoStaticStr from the strum crate, or - maybe better - having a custom trait to represent this).Do what you believe the end-user would find most natural. If what your macro is doing is implementing a trait - you probably ought to make it a derive macro unless you have good reason not to.We’ll talk more about derive macros when we cover procedural macros in a later article, though.

#9986. Mozilla leaves Solo website owners to go it alone as hosting shuts down

If you have one of these AI-generated homepages, you'd better download and save it quick

Solo, Mozilla's LLM-powered website builder and hosting service, is shutting down. All sites and data will be deleted on November 30.

Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. Some 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them – complete with custom domain names.

Well, not any more. Now the Soloist.ai homepage says: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026."

Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ, users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images.

The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com, with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. So much for having the fiddly bits taken care of.

It also points at a couple of other bot-based site-generating services – in case all this feels like a bit too much. We suspect that for the sort of technophobes that this was aimed at, it very probably will.

Mozilla told The Register: "Experimentation is an important part of Mozilla's mission to make the internet better and give people more choice and control online. Sometimes, that means making the decision to bring a product to an end. Solo will officially shut down on November 30, 2026. We initially notified customers on October 1, providing a 60-day transition period, and have been offering support to help them download their website data and migrate their domains purchased via Solo Domains to another hosting provider."

It seems that some 54,000 users were not enough to keep it going, and we can see that this would cost money to keep running. An HTML export is a start, though the FAQ doesn't explain how much work it will take to get a complete, functioning site running elsewhere.

Buried in the dark recesses of the web is this vulture's own nearly 30-year-old homepage, created using a mixture of Claris Home Page (which was excellent) and Microsoft FrontPage (ever so slightly less so). We saw what a mess machine-generated web content was back then, and thanks to LLMs, we suspect it is almost infinitely worse now.

Mozilla might have made a few bucks by finding a commercial partner to take on its users, and perhaps through them offer a paid site-and-domain transfer service. As we noted last year, it seems not to have negotiated anything with KaiOSTech, which maintains and sells what used to be the formerly FOSS FirefoxOS for use on low-end smartphones.

#9985. Run AI workloads on any cloud, store on Hugging Face: zero-egress storage with SkyPilot

For most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud. The GPUs you can get, whether for development, training, or serving, increasingly sit on a different cloud than your data. The moment those two come apart, you pay a cross-cloud transfer tax just to read your own data onto your own GPUs.

Together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs. Mount a Hugging Face Bucket or any Hub repo into a SkyPilot job with one hf:// URL and the HF_TOKEN you already have, then launch it wherever capacity is. Hugging Face charges no egress, so reading your data onto those GPUs costs nothing, on any cloud.

SkyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path. Hugging Face Storage now joins that list as store: hf, reached through the hf:// scheme:

That one hf:// scheme covers the whole lifecycle: read the model and dataset from their repos, write checkpoints to a Bucket while you train, publish the finished model back to a repo, and pull it onto inference servers when you serve. Most teams already keep their models and datasets on the Hub, so there is no migration step and no new storage account to create.

MOUNT uses Hugging Face's hf-mount FUSE backend, so a bucket or repo shows up as a local path next to SkyPilot's other FUSE mounts (gcsfuse, blobfuse2, rclone, goofys). The fetching happens at the filesystem layer: when your code issues a read(), the driver pulls just those bytes from the Xet backend, so only the data you actually touch crosses the network, and hf-mount keeps an on-disk cache so repeat reads stay local. That on-disk cache is the behavior SkyPilot gives its other backends under MOUNT_CACHED, where a plain MOUNT instead streams every read from the bucket with nothing kept locally. For the hf store, MOUNT and MOUNT_CACHED behave the same, so either mode keeps the cache.

Because reads are lazy, a process can start working through a large file before the whole file has downloaded, instead of blocking on a full copy first. That keeps the GPU busy almost immediately, training on data as it streams in rather than sitting idle (and billing) while a dataset or checkpoint copies down. It pays off most on the first epoch, when nothing is cached yet. COPY takes the other route and downloads through huggingface_hub up front, with no special requirements.

Authentication is the token you already have. Set HF_TOKEN in your environment and hand it to a run with --secret HF_TOKEN; SkyPilot uses it for the mount on whatever cloud the job lands. One token works whether the job lands on AWS, GCP, Azure, Nebius, Lambda, or your own Kubernetes cluster, so there are no per-cloud bucket keys to juggle.

GPU capacity rarely comes from one place anymore. To get enough H100s and H200s, teams hold reserved and committed capacity across several vendors at once (a block on a hyperscaler, a cluster on a neocloud, maybe an on-prem rack) and run wherever they have allocation. SkyPilot is built for this: one job spec, scheduled across 20+ clouds, Kubernetes, and on-prem, landing on whichever reserved cluster is free.

Object storage has been the catch. Object stores are regional and per-cloud, so feeding a GPU or an inference server that sits in a different vendor's data center means either keeping a copy of your data in every vendor's bucket or paying to pull it across. Most clouds charge egress (around $0.09/GB out of AWS) the moment data leaves their network, and often between regions inside one cloud. Pulling a base model onto every inference node, or iterating a dataset for several epochs from a cluster on another cloud, adds a hefty bill on top of GPUs you have already reserved. Teams end up pinning each run to whichever vendor holds the data and leaving the rest of their capacity idle.

Hugging Face Storage takes that cost off the table where it bites: the read side. With no egress or CDN fees and storage at $12-18/TB/month (versus AWS S3 at roughly $23/TB plus egress), the same bucket is reachable from every one of those clusters, and reading from it is free no matter where the GPUs run. Writing back still costs your compute cloud's usual egress, the same as it would to any off-cloud store, but for most AI work the reads dominate: a dataset streamed over many epochs, or model weights pulled onto every new training or inference node. So you stop pinning each run to whichever vendor holds a copy of the data.

To collect some benchmark numbers, we ran a small fine-tune: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B on the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset with TRL's SFTTrainer, mounting the model read-only from its Hub repo and writing every checkpoint to a Hugging Face Bucket. The same SkyPilot YAML ran on AWS, GCP, and Lambda, changing only --infra. SkyPilot placed each job wherever GPUs were free, and all three read and wrote the same bucket.

Per cloud, checkpoints wrote to the bucket at:

Hugging Face Buckets are built on Xet, which uses content-defined chunking to split files into ~64 KB chunks and store each unique chunk once. Because the boundaries follow the content, an edit changes only the chunks it touches and the rest are recognized as already stored. This pays off in a few places:

How much you save depends on how much your artifacts overlap, but the deduplication is automatic: you write a checkpoint as usual, and only the new chunks leave the machine.

Add an hf:// mount to any SkyPilot task and launch. MOUNT needs a base image with glibc 2.34+ and /dev/fuse.

The initial store: hf support started as a contribution from Nikhil Jha. The Hugging Face team carried it forward and upstreamed the hf-mount FUSE fixes that let it mount in unprivileged containers, the default on many Kubernetes clusters. The SkyPilot team wired it into the storage backend. The whole path is open source: SkyPilot, Hugging Face's hf-mount, and the huggingface_hub client.

#9984. How Will AI Affect Open Source Development?

The Fine Print: The following comments are owned by whoever posted them. We are not responsible for them in any way.

... but if you don't incorporate AI into your project manage system, you're going to get swamped by it all. AI needs to also handle the first-tier of bug reports, patch submissions, and feature requests - reviewing them, evaluating them within the project goals, filtering out or improving submissions with issues, seeking and taking into account user feedback on controversial issues, etc. The limited human hours that most OSS projects have need to be insulated from the deluge, leaving them to focus on the high-level decisions, with content that they receive to consider being pre-reviewed and pre-considered for suitability to the project.

Otherwise, I don't see how most OSS projects can deal with this in the age of AI. Unless there's going to be some big increase in funding from somewhere?

Unless there is a big increase in funding across the board, how do you expect "most OSS projects" will pay for the bottomless bucket of tokens necessary to have "AI" handle project management, bug reports, patch review, etc etc?

What I expect to actually happen here is that the folks that have been maintaining the non-corporate F/OSS stuff will just walk away altogether and find something more personally rewarding to do with their limited time than subsidise commercial exploitation of their work.

how do you expect "most OSS projects" will pay for the bottomless bucket of tokens necessary to have "AI" handle project management, bug reports, patch review, etc etc?By getting one of the subsidized subscriptions at 20 or 100 US$ from Anthropic / OpenAI (or whoever).That's not bottomless, but a manageable amount of money. But of course it's still money that must come from somewhere and I could definitely understand any OSS developer who doesn't want to pay that.

Deepseek 4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3 Flash, Qwen 3.8 Flash, Muse Ember, Claude 5.5 Haiku, GPT 5.6 Luna, MiMo V2.6 Flash (or even MiMo V2.6 Pro), etc.

You don't need to use, say, Fable or Astra to handle bug reports :P

Also, handling bug reports / patch review is far less token-intensive than coding as well. It's really hard to compete with coding when it comes to token consumption.

That doesn't change the bottom line that tokens cost money that is nearly entirely coming out of maintainers' pockets.

I don't think you understand how cheap these models are.

Combined with the low token usage compared to normal coding, it's a total non-issue. I'll pay for any major OSS project's token usage for project management myself if they ask, that's how little it is.

Simple... they don't cave in and use AI... thus, maintaining the FOSS moniker... soon as you incorporate some "Clod" code into it, it's not FOSS.

Oh, and the free usage for the AIs is going to go away once everyone is addicted enough to it... it already has all your information, so it can just setup a recurring subscription. Not a big deal.

You _could_ refuse all AI junk and just write and release , and figure out an AI-proof bug-reporting system.

Indeed. And on top of that, using LLM code may well compromise the FOSS license used as well. Not good.

My take is that FOSS projects at this time need to reject contributions written in full or major parts by LLMs. In a few years we will know more and can revisit that.

Using AI bug discovery and AI patches is great...For QA and testing, yes, for coding, no. We are increasingly learning that AI coding often does not really save time on serious projects. "AI now writes code almost for free, and that raises a hard question for the whole software industry: if code costs next to nothing, where does the value of software lie?"

For the service the software provides???I mean, you don't pay a guy for the sole act of swinging a hammer, you're paying him because he's building you a house to live in

But open source is often practically oriented. The author's aren't after money or fame, it has close to zero marketing and many projects are "I built a nice tool for me, if you find it helpful you can use it as well". If the helper I put online is getting out of fashion because someone else built the same with more bells and whistles I don't have any disadvantage from it, because I didn't put it online for paying rent.

The same way I don't care too much if you can now clone it with a hand full of LLM prompts. Maybe today I would have built it with a hand full of LLM prompts myself. I may even decide not to put it in online as it is most likely that people will rather create it with AI themselves tailored to their needs than having to deal with how to apply my tool to their use cases.

So no matter if the creation is now free, the product is useful if you need the program. It is only no longer useful to make money of it. That's mostly a problem for closed source. F/OSS doesn't need to "retain relevance".

Does it still itch? Scratch ahead. Did it stop, because someone did better scratching with AI? Great, enjoy your Netflix dinner on the couch! :-)

#9983. Hugging Face Models on Foundry Managed Compute

At Microsoft Build 2026, we announced Foundry Managed Compute and Hugging Face models on Foundry — a curated catalog of open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem, refreshed weekly, deployable in one click onto Foundry Managed Compute. Weights are pre-staged in Azure, runtimes are built and scanned by Microsoft, and every model in the Collection ships with the same enterprise security, governance, observability, and billing that applies to every other model on Foundry.

Microsoft Foundry is a platform for building and operating agentic AI applications. Foundry starts with the widest model selection on any cloud — models from Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, Hugging Face, and others, spanning frontier, open-source, and custom weights — all accessible through a single endpoint and a single set of SDKs in Python, C#, JavaScript, and Java.

On top of those models sits the Foundry Agent Service: multi-agent orchestration with built-in memory, knowledge grounding through Foundry IQ, and a catalog of connectable tools via agentic protocols, so agents can work with enterprise data. Once agents are running, Foundry provides end-to-end tracing, real-time monitoring, continuous evaluations, and a prompt optimizer that improves agent behavior based on eval results — observability and quality loops that are part of the platform.

Alongside that, developers get access to:

Alongside pay-per-token (lowest-friction path to get started) and provisioned throughput (predictable, high-performance production workloads on frontier models), Foundry Managed Compute is the third deployment option in Foundry: a managed GPU platform-as-a-service for open-source and custom models.

You deploy a model instance described by the things that matter to your workload — parameter count, context length, and whether you want to optimize for latency or throughput — and Foundry handles the GPU topology underneath, whether the instance lands on one accelerator or several, so you think and plan in model terms.

Microsoft takes care of the machine: container updates, runtime upgrades, and security patches happen automatically on the supported runtimes — vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, NIM, TEI, llama.cpp — without redeploying your model, while model configuration, deployment behavior, and routing stay with you.

That consistency carries through the developer surface — pay-per-token, provisioned throughput, and Managed Compute share:

Open-source models integrate with Foundry Agents the same way frontier models do, so you can mix model types in a single agent without a separate integration path.

Same code, same workflow. Quota is aligned to accelerator families, so a plan built on the H100 family today carries forward as new hardware generations come online.

Hugging Face is the public square of open AI: 15 million builders, 400,000 organizations, and over 3 million open models published, with new frontier capabilities — agentic coding, video segmentation, speech, embeddings — landing weekly. It's the GitHub of open models, where the community publishes weights, writes model cards, compares evaluations, and pulls models for experimentation.

Open models have closed the gap with proprietary models on benchmark after benchmark, and they unlock things proprietary endpoints can't:

The catch has always been the operational layer: discovery, license review, security screening, runtime selection, GPU sizing, image building, CVE patching, and standing the model up behind an enterprise-grade endpoint. Hugging Face, by itself, is not an enterprise serving platform. Hugging Face models on Foundry is that operational layer, run by Microsoft.

The Hugging Face Collection brings a curated subset of models directly into the Foundry Model Catalog:

From your side, an open-weight model in the Hugging Face Collection looks and behaves like any other model in the Foundry Model Catalog, and every model in the Collection has been put through a multi-stage publishing pipeline before it ever shows up there.

Hugging Face and Microsoft work together to bring the most popular open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem to Microsoft Foundry — production-ready for enterprise environments — through a systematic curation process:

Because weights are pre-staged in Azure storage and runtime images live in a Microsoft-managed registry, your deployments won't need outbound network access to Hugging Face Hub — you can deploy to production inside a private network.

Hugging Face models on Foundry are powered by a versatile collection of community-built, open-source inference runtimes — each selected and tuned for Foundry Managed Compute, and matched to the model architectures it serves best. Across all runtimes, the systematic curation process means new versions and patches land on Foundry quickly, and existing model deployments are upgraded automatically — without requiring you to redeploy.

vLLM — the default high-throughput serving engine for open large language models, tuned for production GPU workloads. Because Hugging Face is a direct contributor to vLLM, any model in the Transformers library can run on vLLM out of the box — so when a new model lands on Hugging Face, it can be served on Foundry the same day, with no waiting on a custom integration.

SGLang — a serving engine for language and multi-modal models, with strong support for structured outputs (JSON, regex, grammar-constrained generation) that agentic and tool-using workloads depend on. Hugging Face and the SGLang team have built a Transformers backend integration for SGLang, so any model in the Transformers library runs on SGLang out of the box — and reaches Foundry the same day it lands on Hugging Face.

Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) — the runtime for embedding, reranker, and sequence-classification models. Accelerator-specific images ship with kernels compiled for each GPU and CPU family Foundry supports, keeping the embedding hot path lean for RAG and semantic-search workloads.

llama.cpp — the CPU and small-GPU path for GGUF-quantized models. Useful for cost-optimized deployments, smaller models, and CPU-only regions, with the same OpenAI-compatible API as vLLM and SGLang.

TensorRT-LLM and NIM — used on NVIDIA hardware where NVIDIA's optimized kernels and Triton-based serving deliver meaningfully better latency or throughput for specific model families.

hf-serve — Hugging Face's own multi-model inference server, used for model architectures outside the LLM and embedding fast paths (vision, audio, segmentation, and other Transformers-native pipelines) so the Collection can cover every modality with a consistent serving layer.

The Hugging Face Collection in the Foundry Model Catalog is where you start, and deployment is five steps:

A deployment template is the unit of choice in step 2: a named, versioned asset that pins the runtime, the accelerator family and count, the context length, and the runtime-specific tuning needed to serve the model well — so picking a template is the only knob you turn for "how do I want this model to run."

qwen3-32b, for example, ships with four templates the deploy wizard exposes side by side:

Each template arrives pre-tuned for the model — runtime settings, tool-call and reasoning parsers, scoring path, health probes, request concurrency, and any model-specific context-extension settings are all set by Microsoft, with any trade-offs called out inline in the template description. When you script the deploy, you reference the template and Foundry handles the rest.

The deployment is reachable through the unified Foundry endpoint with the OpenAI SDK — the `model` field takes the deployment name you just created:

A chat-completions model from the Collection slots into Foundry Agents as an admin-connected model and is callable through the Foundry Responses API with the same OpenAI SDK — same auth, same endpoint, same observability.

Available now in preview: the Hugging Face Collection in the Microsoft Foundry Model Catalog — thousands of models across every modality, refreshed weekly, deployable onto Foundry Managed Compute with NVIDIA A100, NVIDIA H100, or AMD MI300X accelerators in Global and Data Zone scopes, behind a unified Foundry endpoint with Playground support, first-class Azure Monitor metrics, per-deployment billing tags, and curated runtime upgrades and CVE patching applied automatically to your deployments.

On the roadmap: broader coverage of the Hugging Face ecosystem, additional accelerator families, and Bring Your Own Weights for fine-tuned and proprietary variants deployed through the same templates and governance as Collection models.

Hugging Face is where open models are published and discovered. Microsoft Foundry is where enterprises operationalize them — on curated, license-screened, security-screened weights hosted in Azure; on community-built and CVE-scanned runtimes; behind a single endpoint with enterprise identity, networking, observability, and agent integration on top. The breadth of the open-source ecosystem, with the operational layer Microsoft runs underneath. For a deep dive on Foundry Managed Compute — pricing, accelerator SKUs, data residency, enterprise readiness, observability, and the full Responses API + memory pattern — see the Managed Compute launch blog.
