#9969. FAA blames ground stop on faulty copper wiring

Safety reasons and unspecified communications issue cited

The US Federal Aviation Administration on Friday issued an advisory that prevented the takeoff of flights in US airspace for around five hours, creating chaos for travelers and airports. The stop was finally lifted around 8:30 PM Eastern Time, but only after thousands of flights were canceled or delayed, leaving travelers stranded.

In a press conference Saturday, Transportation Secretary Duffy attributed the FAA ground stop to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade. Duffy said it has yet to be determined whether the issue was incompetence or a faulty router.

In a statement provided to The Register on Saturday, a spokesperson for L3Harris said, “L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70 percent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

The stop was issued on Friday around the middle of the day ET.

"The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a statement on Friday. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them."

A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone at the time said he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement.

The FAA ATCSCC advisory halted departing flights and said international flights would be dealt with individually.

The notice said, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis."

Doug Yakel, public information officer for San Francisco International Airport, said, "FAA confirms nationwide ground stop, other reporting indicates a communications issue between Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Aircraft already enroute to SFO still landing here but departing aircraft not taking off right now."

An update issued at 2:02 pm PT described the problem as "a temporary telecommunications outage."

The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) is managed by L3Harris. The network provides secure communication between more than 4,400 facilities. ®

Updated at 0039 UTC Sunday UTC with the administration's explanation for the stop.

Updated at 0211 Saturday UTC to reflect the lifting of the ground stop.

CBS News reports that “an update to the private communications network that connects America’s air traffic control system caused the system to reboot. When the FAA’s telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage. The system is operated by L3Harris.”

Air Space Intelligence (ASI), awarded the FAA’s $875 million, 12-year contract for its new Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system, has issued a statement asserting that its products played no role in the FAA’s flight suspension. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

#9967. Periodic-Oriented Programming for FIRST Robotics

I recently retired from mentoring my FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) team. I started as a student in 2010, and went straight into mentoring upon graduation, so in total I have been writing FRC programs for about 17 years.

Over time though I've become more and more dismayed with how FRC programs are typically written. For decades, I feel that FIRST and WPILib have encouraged students to severely overengineer their robot programs. As time has gone on, I have become more and more frustrated with the state of FRC programming, and our team's code style has drifted further and further away from the norm.

To be clear, I have the utmost respect for the time and effort that FIRST and the WPILib maintainers put in every year, and it is thanks to their efforts that FRC teams have reliable and complete libraries every year. But I think the accepted programming practices in FRC are leading students astray and ought to be corrected.

So as I step away from FIRST, I decided I should write down my philosophy of robot programming in FRC, which I have decided to give the pithy name of Periodic-Oriented Programming.

Periodic-Oriented Programming is very simple: Do as much as possible in your periodic function. Uses very few abstractions, and write most of your logic in one big function, top to bottom. This is so simple and beginner-like that it seems like it shouldn't work for serious programs. But it does, as long as you carefully establish a few simple boundaries and practices.

For context, the essential structure of an FRC program is typically to use the TimedRobot framework provided by WPILib. To use it, you simply implement periodic functions and the robot framework calls them 50 times per second. For example, here's a complete "tank drive" robot program in Python:

50 times per second, the left and right motor speeds will be updated to use the left and right gamepad axes. The robot framework and hardware abstraction layers do the rest.

In essence, every FRC program does the following work in periodic:

In Periodic-Oriented Programming, I basically encourage my students to lean into this pattern. POP code should have few abstractions, and most of the logic should be written top-to-bottom in a single function. And to the greatest extent possible, everything should be run on every periodic—no modes, no commands, no state.

As programs get larger, more structure is needed, but the core philosophy remains the same. The most important piece of structure is subsystems.

The use of "subsystem" classes will be familiar to most FRC teams, but the specifics are what matter here:

These rules extend the Periodic-Orientation into the subsystem code. For each subsystem, all of its logic should be centralized in one function and readable top to bottom. In most cases, the subsystem periodic is the only place in the entire program that actually touches the hardware. This has many advantages: it ensures by construction that hardware is only touched once per tick, that safety constraints are respected 100% of the time, and that logging and telemetry are run consistently.

Centralizing most logic in periodic also provides a nice platform for both autonomous and teleoperated code. The subsystem's API surface can be comprised of very high-level functions like driveFieldRelative(vx, vy) or goToElevatorPreset(coralOrAlgae, level), which basically just set instance variables to be read later in periodic. These subsystem functions also provide a consistent place to validate inputs (e.g. impossible speeds, angles, or presets), convert units, etc.

By the way, don't be afraid to combine two subsystems if their logic is intertwined. For example, in 2025 our robot had an arm on an elevator, and the safe angles for the arm were dependent on the height of the elevator. Therefore, we made a combined ElevatorAndArm subsystem. (If you've heard advice that classes should be about "one thing", ignore that advice, it is wrong.[1])

As I described earlier, every FRC program computes the desired state of the hardware, then updates the outputs to move in that direction. This is most obviously true of closed-loop control (PID, typically), where you simply set a target value (e.g. "elevator at 6 feet") and then compute outputs that will move the hardware toward that target.

Successful Periodic-Oriented programs apply this philosophy to the entire robot program. What hardware state do I want, and how do I get there? This way of thinking applies at the actuator level (e.g. motor speeds), the mechanism level (e.g. arm angles), and the whole-robot level (e.g. safety constraints like "arm can only go out when elevator is down"). It is universal to all robot control.

The question of "What hardware state do I want?" falls naturally into teleopPeriodic and autonomousPeriodic. They naturally define answers to questions like: Where on the field? What velocity? What elevator position? What arm angle? What shooter RPM?

The question of "How do I get there?" then falls naturally into a subsystem periodic. Often it is as simple as elevatorMotor.setReference(elevatorHeight), deferring the actual closed-loop behavior to your motor controllers. But extra behaviors can easily be layered in here too; for example, the whole-robot constraint described earlier can be as simple as:

Or you could do a "state machine" approach, where attempting to put the arm out will actually drop the elevator to a safe position first:

In a Periodic-Oriented program, complex behaviors like this are easy to debug, robustly uphold safety constraints, never produce conflicting outputs to hardware, and often require less state than other approaches. Speaking of:

Robots have enough state to deal with in the real world. So don't add extra state to your program!

For the beginners in the audience, "state" in programming is data in your program that changes over time. Common sources of state in FRC programs include:

Some of these are inherent, such as the physical robot state (which is the entire point). Others are not, such as modes. It is well-known in programming, across many domains, that more state == more problems, so remove or isolate state wherever you can:

Avoid autonomous state. For most teams, it is very viable to represent all autonomous outputs as a function of time. In the extreme, this might look like:

But while this looks silly, this is more or less what tools like Choreo let you do. A Choreo trajectory is just a list of desired positions, velocities, and actions for the robot over time, and executing a Choreo trajectory is literally as simple as looking up the current desired state and applying it to your drivetrain. (This is also true of PathPlanner, but to a lesser extent due to its dependence on commands.)

And it need not be fancy: In 2011, when I was a student, my dad (an industrial automation engineer) advised me to author our autonomous routines in spreadsheets. Each autonomous routine that year was literally a CSV file, with one column per actuator and one row per "step" (with start and end times). At any given time, you could simply look up the current row of the table, and look at each column to see what each motor's output should be. It worked well! I don't know why we never did it again.

And there is one final piece of advice that eclipses all others:

The WPILib "command-based" programming system is an unmitigated disaster that should never be used under any circumstances.

Harsh? Yes. But after writing and teaching command-based code for ten years, then trying other approaches for another seven, I have concluded that the command-based approach is almost entirely without merit.

At its heart, the problem with the command-based system is that it is woefully, impossibly stateful. When using commands, you don't know which commands are currently active in the scheduler, you don't know what order they execute in, it's difficult to predict when they start, and it's all but impossible to know when they end.

I have witnessed three generations of students (myself included), across multiple teams, debugging bizarre and entirely artificial problems caused entirely by the command-based system. "Why can't we run autonomous twice? Oh, because you can't always call initialize after end? Maybe I need to construct a new command instance? But how can I do that if onTrue takes a Command instead of a () -> Command? Why did the robot stop driving? Oh, something canceled the Drivetrain subsystem's default command? I guess it shouldn't require the subsystem then? Oh, I guess now we're setting the motor speeds twice? Why did that one run before the default command?"

I could keep going. "Why did the robot shoot just then? Wait, there was still a command running from earlier in autonomous? Why didn't it get canceled?" Every one of these questions is a stupid waste of time.

The other problem with commands is that they spread once-simple logic across dozens of files. This is purportedly a benefit of using commands, but the reality is that neither students nor mentors are good at piecing all the logic together in their head again. When you have a bug at competition and need to make a code change now, you need code that is brutally simple, where you can be confident that your change won't have unexpected side effects. Straight-line code is better for this purpose.

The remaining advantages for the command-based model are that they make it easier to sequence and schedule actions in autonomous, and that in principle they prevent multiple pieces of logic from accessing the hardware simultaneously. But as I've already suggested, a stateless, time-driven approach to autonomous works better in most situations, intra-subsystem state can be handled in periodic, and the periodic approach avoids the need for the requirements system by construction. (And if you want to ensure that a subsystem method is called only once per periodic, this can be easily achieved with a flag and a log message in the subsystem method itself.)

So, although it might seem crazy, I strongly encourage everyone to avoid command-based programming.

Let me conclude with a snippet of real teleopPeriodic code from our 2025 codebase:

There is no subsystem default command, just a function call. There are no separate commands for field vs. robot relative, just an if statement. There is no separate command or global state for precision controls, just an if statement. There is no binding of commands to buttons, just if statements. Reversed field-relative coordinates for the red alliance? If statement.

Does this feel ugly to you? If so, think of this an acquired taste! This is 25 lines of dead-simple code that completely encapsulates all of our teleop driving logic. The command-based alternative would probably be several classes and 100 to 200 lines of code (when you count all the boilerplate). Here there is no possibility of command cancellation, bad defaults, incorrect execution order, or conflicting writes to the hardware. Instead the code expresses the logic directly and simply.

I suspect that many readers will think this is too simple, like surely this approach will cause problems in practice. But it doesn't! This is our actual 2025 robot code, which supported field-relative and robot-relative swerve drive, odometry and vision, and multiple Choreo-based autonomous routines with different starting points and scoring positions. If you are Orbit and your strategy is 100% autonomous game piece retrieval and placement, then feel free to ignore me. But I believe this approach to FRC programming would be successful for at least 95% of all FRC teams.

[1]The problem with advice like "classes should do one thing, and do it well" is that no one can describe what "one thing" is. This is even acknowledged in books like Clean Code but not clarified in a way I find satisfactory. It is therefore not actionable advice. The decision of where to draw an API boundary should instead be determined by the amount of information that has to cross that boundary. In our ElevatorAndArm example, we could indeed have separated the Elevator and Arm into separate subsystems, but our "coral level 3" preset would then have required calls to two separate subsystems, and both subsystems would have needed references to each other in order to maintain safety constraints. When two classes are deeply aware of each other's internals, you should just combine them.

#9966. Welcome Inkling by Thinking Machines

Update: Inkling 2 Small is here! 🤗 Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Small, the next generation of the Inkling family. We have updated this post with a new section on Inkling 2 Small, covering what changed in the architecture and how to run it with transformers.

Inkling is Thinking Machines' family of open multimodal models, and it now spans two generations on the Hub:

In this post, we start with the first-generation architecture, then walk through what changed in Inkling 2 Small and how to run it. The rest of the post covers inference, use cases, post-training, and deployment, with examples built on the first-generation checkpoints.

Inkling is the first large open model with ~1T parameters and 1M context window to natively receive image, text, and audio inputs, trained on 45 trillion tokens of text, images, audio and video. It’s focused on reasoning across modalities such as audio, images, and text. It is intended for domain adaptation via fine-tuning. We’ve tinkered (pun intended) with this model to build some demos and explore the architecture, and we think it’s great for building a new wave of multimodal reasoning apps.

Inkling is a decoder-only multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) model with 975B total and 41B active parameters. There are a lot of things going on, so let’s break each part down:

Here’s a quick glance of the architecture.

Relative attention: Instead of RoPE, which is the usual method to inject positional information in transformers models, Inkling uses relative attention to encode position information. Each attention layer learns position directly in the attention logits. Aside from key-query-values, there's a fourth projection producing a per-token, per-head relative feature R. This projection tensor is then tweaked with distance information (distance between the key and the query vector) and propagated into the attention module.

Hybrid attention: The decoder layers alternate between global attention (attending to the full context length at once) and sliding window attention (attending to a fixed context window in a sliding fashion). The architecture has a pattern of 5:1 sliding window to global attention layers. This hybrid attention scheme provides efficiency in computation. The final layer uses global attention to help build feature-rich representations.

Short convolution: The model uses a distinctive short 1D convolution, or SConv over the hidden states. SConv reads the current token and the previous W-1 hidden states, with W being the sliding window size. The intuition here is that SConv helps with local attention while freeing the attention and MoE modules from local representations.

MoE with shared experts sink: In Inkling, the router scores both routed experts and shared experts. Top-k selection is performed over 6 experts, plus 2 shared experts always active.

Vision understanding: The model includes a simple hierarchical MLP patchifier consisting of several linear layers. Each layer merges pixels progressively, until the final layer produces one embedding per patch.

Audio understanding: The architecture employs a discretized mel spectrogram, where each of the audio chunks (of 100 ms) are converted to the mel scale and then classified into the exact mel spectrogram bin.

The multimodal towers are relatively simple modules, unlike other models that employ separate encoders for each modality. Each image patch passes through the image embedding tower and the audio chunk is passed through the audio embedding tower to get both media embeddings. Image inputs also include an additional temporal dimension for video processing. We expect this capability to be useful for downstream fine-tuning, but we haven’t evaluated out-of-the-box video performance. The tower folds the patch grid, a small local block of neighboring tokens is stacked into the channel dimension and goes through hMLP. The audio waveform is converted to mel scale, which is then classified into a discrete mel bin. These mel bin values are embedded in the audio embedding tower and the embeddings are then summed to construct the final audio input.

Inkling 2 is the next generation of the family. It takes text and image inputs (but no audio), and generates text. It keeps the core ideas of Inkling's decoder:

Almost everything around that core was redesigned, though. The layers read from the residual stream differently, attention is bounded and gated, the MoE is simpler and wider, and the vision tower is now a real vision transformer.

Let's go over the most notable changes together:

Block attention residuals: In a standard transformer, every layer adds its output to the residual stream, and the next layer reads it. Inkling 2 has no single residual stream. Instead, it groups its 48 layers into 8 blocks of 6 and keeps one sum per block:

A sublayer (attention or MLP) doesn't read one of these sums directly. It attends over depth, which means at each token position, it treats the finished block summaries plus the current partial block as a short sequence, and takes a softmax-weighted mix of them.

The query is a single learned vector per sublayer. The keys and values are the RMS-normalized block summaries at that position. So the weights differ from token to token, depending on what each block wrote there.

In other words, each sublayer learns how much to draw from each earlier stage of the network, rather than always reading the sum of everything. By the last layer, there are up to 9 sources to choose from (the embeddings, 7 finished blocks and the current partial block), and the final norm reads its input the same way. Global attention layers learn three queries, so their query, key and value projections can each draw on a different mix of blocks.

Dynamic short convolutions: The short convolutions on keys and values in the global attention layers are now dynamic. The 4 taps of each convolution are a fixed learned weight plus a per-token weight predicted from the input, shared within each key/value head. So the model can change, token by token, how much local context goes into each key and value. All short convolutions also rescale their residual sum to keep its variance stable through depth.

A leaner, wider MoE: Each layer has 384 routed experts with 8 active per token, and the shared experts are gone.

A new vision encoder: Inkling encoded images with a lightweight hierarchical MLP. Inkling 2 uses a 23-layer vision transformer based on the Perception Encoder. It has the following properties:

Several images are packed into one sequence, and each image only attends to itself.

Inkling 2 uses the same Auto classes as Inkling. Make sure to have updated transformers to run the model.

Inkling comes with day-0 transformers support and is supported in major inference engines like SGLang and vLLM.

This model is huge. The bf16 checkpoint requires 2 TB of VRAM, while the nvfp4 version requires 600 GB of VRAM. You can try the model through serverless inference routers like Inference Providers, or use ggml quants for local deployment with llama.cpp.

The easiest way to infer with transformers directly is to use the any-to-any pipeline. You can use either the 16 bit "thinkingmachines/Inkling" on Hopper or later GPUs, or the quantized NVFP4 checkpoint "thinkingmachines/Inkling-NVFP4" on Blackwell Nvidia GPUs. Make sure to have the latest version of transformers (5.14.0 was released today) (pip install -U transformers).

After initializing the pipeline, you can pass in the prompt as follows.

Going one level lower, you can use Auto classes. For inference, you can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class for models and AutoProcessor class for processors. For different reasoning tasks, the tokenizer takes in a reasoning_effort argument. Existing options for reasoning effort are "none", "minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", and "max".

For multimodal inference, you can use the same classes. We provide example snippets for each different modality in the model card.

Inkling also takes in audio input. Below is an example inference snippet, which still uses the same AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

For more realistic parallel deployment in a cluster of several nodes, please refer to the Slurm section below.

SGLang is one of the fastest deployment frameworks for Inkling at the time of release, as it includes a custom model implementation. The launch command below shards the model across 8 GPUs and serves an OpenAI-compatible API on port 30000.

Match --tp-size to your GPU count. Add --mem-fraction-static (e.g. 0.85) if you need to leave more headroom for the KV cache.

vLLM is strong for production serving. A single vllm serve command downloads the weights from the Hub, shards the model across your GPUs with tensor parallelism, and starts an OpenAI-compatible server on port 8000. You can view the vLLM Recipe for the model here to customize to your hardware.

In practice, you might need multiple nodes and a distribution tool like SLURM (see below). Key parameters are --tensor-parallel-size to the number of GPUs on your node, and use --max-model-len to cap the context window if you hit KV-cache memory limits.

You can infer with this model using several inference providers through Hugging Face. You can see all the code snippets to consume here. Below you can see how to use with the OpenAI client.

Using the “:auto” suffix routes to your preferred provider in your settings; you can also use “cheapest” or “:fastest” as well. For this release, we cover the inference costs for 2 hours within the release for everyone.

Note: audio support in Inference Providers is work in progress and will be added shortly.

You can use llama.cpp to run quantized versions of the model on limited hardware. Unsloth have quantized the model down to 1-bit precision, reducing VRAM consumption by 95% over the original model.

This starts an OpenAI-compatible server running at http://localhost:8080/v1 that you connect to in your preferred tool or clients. Heading there, you can start chatting with the model, and set it up with your favorite MCPs, pass in images or files conveniently and more!

Llama cpp also ships with a built-in UI that supports tools, mcp, and agentic workloads. Checkout Inkling running at 1-bit precision in the llama app:

Inkling GGUFs are also runnable in Unsloth Studio with dynamic 1-bit GGUFs which retain ~74.2% of top-1% accuracy whilst being 86% smaller.

Pi is a minimal coding agent harness you can use with different language models. You can use Pi with either an inference engine server endpoint, such as llama.cpp, or with Inference Providers on Hugging Face by adding this to your ~/.pi/agent/models.json after installation.

Then you can start Pi in your project directory by calling pi and you’re good to go! In this demo, we give the model a hard math reasoning problem and it uses tools in pi to solve it.

Inkling is focused on broad multimodality reasoning and low token consumption, so try it out with document processing or audio tasks.

MTP adds extra layers to the model that predict several tokens at once, not just the next one. During inference, the extra layers act as “drafters” for speculative decoding, speeding up generation without compromising performance. With MTP, you get the exact same generated outputs, multipliers in generation speed-up at small memory cost in VRAM (due to serving the drafter). Thinking Machines also provides an MTP drafter with this release.

We have prepared a small suite of reasoning questions from expert-level sources and university entrance exams. We have taken photos of the screen with watermarks in the screenshot to challenge the model. The model has solved all of them on high one, failed one in highest and medium reasoning efforts, so we provide a link to the model answers for you to check out how the model sounds and provide the number of tokens the model has taken to solve each of them. Note that we provide no system prompts in these vibe evals, and these reasoning questions should often be run with a good system prompt. The vibe eval images and results live here.

We have vibe-evaluated the model on some audio reasoning examples from BigBenchAudio and a few multilingual audio examples of GlobeAudio (Russian and Chinese multi-choice questions asking the last word in transcription). The BigBenchAudio examples we tested consist of logical statements and questions that either ask for formal fallacies (whether an argument can be logically deduced from the context given in audio) or object counting (stating multiple distinctive objects in the audio, asking for the total count of a certain one). Although this benchmark is initially made for speech-to-speech reasoning, we just want to see audio reasoning capabilities of this model. For GlobeAudio, the questions are relatively straightforward, so we ran with reasoning efforts of 0.1. We ran the first example of each language within GlobeAudio. All tests pass on all questions and efforts, except for second formal fallacy example on lowest effort, so we only provide the number of tokens spent in each question against reasoning effort. Vibe eval results and audio files live here.

If you would like to use Inkling for post-training, Thinking Machines have built tinker, a managed tool for post-training open weight models. Their cookbook includes examples for fine-tuning, distillation, and reinforcement learning.

We post trained Inkling with tinker and OpenEnv, an agentic RL environment tool. We used the ECHO algorithm that trains a model to predict the environment without a verifier, applying next-token cross-entropy loss to tokens produced by the environment, alongside the usual policy learning on agent actions. This teaches the policy an implicit world model without requiring a separate model, teacher, or additional rollouts. Check out the example.

If you’re working with Transformers Reinforcement Learning we suggest using Inkling as a teacher model in a knowledge distillation setup. For example, take advantage of Inkling’s document understanding abilities to improve the performance of a smaller (on-device) model. In this example, we use the transformer reinforcement learning library and the GOLD algorithm to distill knowledge. GOLD is handy here because it matches token logits between different tokenizers, so you can distill to any model on the hub.

Below you can find each Inkling checkpoint as well as their VRAM requirements.

To deploy Inkling on a cluster, we provide SLURM scripts serving with transformers API, as well as how to query the endpoint with different modalities. You can adapt these scripts to vLLM or SGlang by updating the commands. These scripts live here.

You can deploy an Inkling-Small NVFP4 checkpoint using Inference Endpoints. We provide a pre-tested configuration to deploy it on 8 RTX PRO 6000s with an aggregated VRAM of·768 GB, giving large space for KV cache, costs $ 22 per hourly uptime (scales to zero when unused). To deploy, run hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4 using the Hugging Face CLI or alternatively, head to https://endpoints.huggingface.co/new/thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4. With this setup, you can get 140 TPS (single user inference, prepared for multi-user support with continuous batching)

Once the endpoint is up, you can query as follows.

Releasing a natively multimodal model (text, vision, and audio) open-weights is a huge step forward for the open-source AI ecosystem! Having variable and controllable thinking effort built into a MoE architecture makes Inkling a really attractive foundation for fine-tuning. Excited to test out the smaller 12B active parameter variant for local agent workflows at https://geometrydashsubzero.io

#9965. Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum

Accessing banned content is as easy as whipping out a thesaurus, Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee hears

Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say.

A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters.

Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms.

"Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said.

"I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable.

"So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently."

McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not.

"If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added.

Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too.

Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal.

She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly.

There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs.

"So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content."

Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories.

With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process.

As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially.

Citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent.

Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures.

The charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if the report comes from an authority like Refuge, it is acted upon more quickly.

Walker said there was real concern about how platforms behave and whether they comply with existing regulation, and about what that means for specialist services supporting survivors in limbo, particularly without an online commission to advocate for victims' and survivors' interests.

Meta did not immediately respond to questions about its takedown rate, but according to its Community Standards Enforcement Report, it removed 27.8 million posts related to adult nudity and sexual activity between April and June 2026. The report does not include a category devoted to VAWG-related reports, so take the data with the appropriate level of scrutiny.

Neither Google, Microsoft, nor TikTok responded to requests for comment.

The findings from Refuge and the discussion in Parliament this week reflect the wider concern about the efficacy of the OSA, and how online safety experts are frustrated with how little impact it has had, more than a year after the new duties came into force.

England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same committee in September that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference" to children's access to harmful content online, as evidenced by the accounts of young people themselves.

Amid discussions from the panel of experts this week regarding the need for a civil redress scheme, McGlynn pointed to British Columbia's system as an example of how other countries are going further to protect people from online harms.

She said: "...an individual still does not have the right to demand an image be taken down. And that is where I think we just lack that capacity to say to an individual, 'this is what you need to do, and you can bring this legal action, for example, against X, against the perpetrator, you can get the material deleted.'

"In British Columbia in Canada, they have a swift online civil redress system where you can make these claims, and you can get instant orders to get this material taken down, and you can even get compensation for some of the harm suffered.

"So other countries are doing more, if you like, to give the individuals that right as well as all the other measures at the platform level." ®

The Fine Print: The following comments are owned by whoever posted them. We are not responsible for them in any way.

Humans evolved to survive in a violent world. Those instincts haven't simply evaporated after a few decades of cultural enlightenment.

It is far preferable to allow those instincts to find expression in a completely harmless video game than out in the real world. Channeling violence in this way eliminates stress and brings players back to a position of emotional balance from which they can cope with the burdens of everyday life. It also has side-effects of improving cognitive health and helping to build and solidify communities of friendship.

The overt themes are distasteful because they depict aspects of the real world that we don't like. But that's also what makes the game effective in providing a healthy outlet for the very instincts that can create those tragedies. The many studies that have been done on the topic have always given the same results: playing violent video games does not make people violent. The harm that the haters complain about simply isn't there, according to consciously-obtained data.

You are free to find your own balance. But before sitting in judgment of those who find playing games like this to be anodyne for the soul, maybe take the time to reflect on what life might be like for people in other circumstances than your own, and how something like this might be a net social benefit.

#9963. Model Routing Is Simple. Until It Isn’t.

Building a router into your agent sounds like an easy win. Send simple requests to cheaper models, reserve expensive ones for harder tasks, or route by specialty — Claude for code, Gemini for multimodal, and so on. A classifier or heuristic makes the call, costs go down, performance stays up. Done.

Except it’s not. Most routing systems assume that model selection is a classification problem. In our experience building routing into agentic systems, what looks like a model-selection problem quickly becomes a systems optimization problem. Three dimensions made this surprisingly hard for us.

We expected GPT-4.1 to be cheaper than Claude Sonnet 4.6. It wasn’t.

Across 417 tasks on the AppWorld Test Challenge using the same CodeAct agent, Sonnet cost $79 total ($0.19/task) while GPT-4.1 cost $155 ($0.37/task) — nearly double. On paper, this makes no sense. GPT-4.1’s token pricing is lower on both input and output, and Sonnet takes roughly three times as many reasoning steps to finish the same tasks. By sticker price alone, GPT-4.1 should win easily.

The explanation? Caching — something most routing discussions ignore entirely. Agent workloads tend to reuse large chunks of context across steps. When cache hit rates are high, effective input costs drop dramatically. Sonnet’s lower cache-read pricing meant it benefited disproportionately from this pattern, enough to overcome both its higher base pricing and its longer trajectories.

The takeaway: actual cost depends on the interaction between the model, the workload, and the serving infrastructure. A router that only looks at pricing sheets is optimizing against the wrong numbers.

A common routing strategy is to estimate how hard a task is and send harder tasks to stronger models. Intuitive, but it breaks down in two ways.

First, difficulty is often invisible at routing time. A request like "summarize this contract" looks simple, but might trigger retrieval, compliance checks, tool use, and multiple rounds of refinement before it’s done. Meanwhile, a highly technical prompt might be handled efficiently by a smaller specialized model. You often don’t know how hard a task actually is until execution is underway.

Routers aren’t solving one problem. They’re constantly juggling cost, quality, latency, compliance, and reliability all at once.

It’s tempting to think about latency purely in terms of model size — bigger models are slower, smaller ones are faster. But what the user actually experiences depends on much more than that.

Routing itself adds overhead. Infrastructure factors — which hardware a model is running on, whether the cache is warm, how busy the endpoint is — often dominate end-to-end response times. A theoretically faster model can still produce a slower experience if the serving conditions aren’t right.

Then there’s routing granularity. Routing once per task adds minimal overhead. But routing at every step — which gives you more flexibility to adapt mid-execution — means every additional decision point introduces latency and operational complexity.

A router that ignores the serving system is optimizing against the wrong reality.

These lessons shaped how we built our router. The key shift: we stopped treating routing as a classification problem and started treating it as an optimization problem. Rather than asking "which model is best for this task?", our algorithm optimizes across cost, quality, and latency simultaneously — while staying lightweight enough to avoid becoming a bottleneck itself.

The figure below shows the result on the AppWorld Test Challenge with a CodeAct agent. Each blue square is a different configuration of our router, tracing out a cost-accuracy frontier. The important thing isn't any single point — it's that the router gives you a range of operating points to choose from depending on whether you want to prioritize cost, latency, or accuracy. Configuration 1 (latency-optimized) lands at 84% accuracy for $93 and 83s — a 21% cost reduction and 9% latency reduction compared to running Opus alone, with only a 4% accuracy drop. Configuration 2 pushes cost even lower.

Notice that a standard difficulty-based router (the teal diamond) lands in a similar accuracy range but at higher cost — it doesn't explore the full tradeoff space the way an optimization-based approach can. And because the optimization itself is lightweight (roughly 6 ms and 2 kB of memory per task), the router doesn't become the bottleneck we warned about earlier.

The lesson we took away from this work is that routing isn’t really about choosing models. It’s about optimizing systems. Models are one variable — an important one, but just one among caching behavior, infrastructure state, compliance constraints, and workload patterns.

When routing works well, it’s rarely because it found the "best" model for a given task. It’s because it found the best operating point for the entire system. That’s a harder problem than classification, but it’s the one worth solving.

We’ll be sharing more about the technical details behind our approach in a follow-up post. In the meantime, if you’re building routing into your own agentic systems, we’d love to hear what tradeoffs you’re running into.

This post was influenced by numerous conversations with colleagues, whose thoughtful questions, feedback, and insights helped refine our thinking.

So I've always felt that model routing is a false proposition; it should have been part of the harness all along.

Agreed, routing should disappear into the harness and just be part of the system's execution logic. Our goal is exactly that—making model choice an intrinsic capability rather than a separate concern.

#9962. Microsoft's school email bill gives rivals something to smile about

Collabora and Nextcloud pitch alternatives as education customers weigh the cost of losing free services

The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces.

The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news.

As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like. Or, for that matter, other US tech giants.

Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners.

The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks.

A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill.

Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud."

A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't."

The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly."

Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure. Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted.

Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty.

Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register: "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure.

"Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy."

Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service. But the Windows behemoth has given educational institutions a fresh reason to investigate – and its rivals a particularly convenient opening pitch. ®

#9961. Designing nextest's install scripts

Four and a half years after I released the first version of cargo-nextest, it now has install scripts! This has been a long time coming, and I’m really happy to finally have support for them.

On Unix-like platforms, including WSL, Cygwin, and Git Bash for Windows (MSYS), you can now run install.sh:

On Windows, you can also use PowerShell with install.ps1:

I wanted to write a bit about why it took so long to publish them, how they work, and how I used coding agents to meet a high quality bar.

We’ve published release binaries for the nextest project since its very earliest versions in 2022. When initially designing support for release binaries, I spent some time looking at the options for how to deliver them to users. The usual approach is an install script that you curl | sh or irm | iex, but I determined that:

Based on this, I came up with an alternate approach: produce tarballs (and a zip file for Windows), and ask people to extract it themselves. For example, on Linux, you would run:

But over time, the cracks started to show: while the Unix shell instructions were a single line, the Windows instructions were a five-line mess. There wasn’t a single command that worked on any platform, so nothing that could be shown on the home page. Also, on Linux, there was no way to select a statically-linked musl build automatically if the system version of glibc was too old or not present.

I felt that install scripts were going to be needed in the long term. This year, over a month of intermittent work, I finally put together a pretty solid pair of scripts. They’re tested to work in a wide variety of situations under many different failure modes, and I feel quite confident they meet the quality bar set by the rest of nextest. (The manual archive extraction path will continue to work as well.)

Mukti has been extended to produce a text file containing archive URLs and checksums for each version, called an install manifest (example for the latest version). The manifest is designed to be easily parseable with standard word-splitting utilities present on every system, like read in Unix shells and -split in PowerShell.

The shell script works with any Bourne shell, and the PowerShell script runs on both the legacy (but installed by default on Windows) version 5.1 and the new PowerShell 7. They follow a series of steps:

As I expected, a production-ready install script has to deal with a surprising amount of complexity. Some examples:

The install process, such as the manifest format and location at well-known URLs, was very much designed by me. I had a ton of implementation and testing help from Claude Code and Codex, though.

One way to use them, which I’m going to call the vibed approach, is:

This is how you end up with install scripts with hundreds of lines of repetitive sections. Earlier this year, a popular project’s install script became a somewhat notorious example of this pattern.

But this vibed approach is not how I develop software meant to be used by others. For one, nextest is not my full-time job, and I don’t want to be chasing down a steady stream of issues filed against it. More importantly, I find this approach to building infrastructure-grade software, whatever technical merits it might or might not have, to be against my values. I’m not going to give up my values in service of getting something like this out quicker.

So how did I end up using LLMs for this? Very carefully, and in a way that aimed to increase the level of rigor compared to writing the script by hand.

On the LLM side, by far the most effort went into validation. From my experience with projects at work, I knew that LLMs can be very thorough at building test harnesses that would otherwise require weeks of sustained effort. So, very early on, I decided to build an automated test harness for the installer script. The test harness defines dozens of cases with expected inputs and behaviors, and runs them on a variety of shells. The harness also has:

All of these are well within my capacity to build in principle, though not in any reasonable amount of time. But once the high-level properties one wants to test, such as timeouts on a stalled download, are defined, LLMs are very good at this kind of fill-in-the-blanks semantic infill.

The other large bit of work was on the human side, with design review. Over time, as I’ve gained experience with agentic tools, I’ve settled on a fairly particular — some might say peculiar — way of using them. I first run any code through automated review3 with two different LLMs. After that, I spend a lot of time manually reviewing the code.

How do I make sure I pay attention to the code I’m reviewing? For me, the most effective technique has been to ban the agents from writing comments without a special marker. To be honest, I can’t stand LLM-authored technical writing, and the comments these tools produce are uniformly terrible. But also, when I’m forced to write about how or why some code is written the way it is, I’ve consistently found a startling number of issues. Some that I found in this effort:

The tests were incredibly comprehensive at validating all the possible non-default options, but there were no tests for the most basic no-option happy path. I realized this around a third of the way into the review, and did a major rework of the test harness based on it.

In the test harness, SHA-256 hashes were represented as Rust Strings, and the tests did a weird case-insensitive comparison. I replaced it with the byte-wrapper crate I wrote for Oxide, which provides a HexArray newtype4.

The scripts initially permitted HTTPS to HTTP redirects, and the tests validated that this scenario works. That is completely wrong, of course. Such redirects are now banned.

The Unix tests validated that signals performed cleanup, but there were originally no Ctrl-C tests on Windows. There are now tests for that.

A common theme across many of the defects is that an LLM will often pick a hill to climb, then climb it as thoroughly as possible, without asking whether it is the right hill to climb in the first place. The HTTPS to HTTP redirects are a rather striking example of that: at some point, Claude decided that this is what the script should do, then encoded it in the test suite. The automated review done by subsequent Claude and GPT instances likely led them to conclude “oh, the tests verify that such redirects work — clearly this must be intended behavior”. It requires human wisdom to judge that no, this is wrong.

All in all, the manual review took around 25 hours over 4 weekends. The final result was a change of around 10,000 lines of code, most of which is tests — very different from the initial work done by the LLM, and something I believe I can stand behind. I’m sure there will be a few bugfixes here and there, and maybe major feature work at some point, but overall I consider this work to be completed.

The work is generically implemented in mukti and reusable by other projects, too. I’m not totally sure mukti is fit for public consumption yet, but it’s not too far off. Given how well this works, it might finally be time to push mukti over the line. Maybe over the holidays!

If a thing is worth doing, is it worth doing well? Or should you do it badly? The software industry has gone through a remarkable transformation over the last year. To my dismay, a lot of people who really should know better have chosen the latter. I’m not saying there isn’t a place for that, but I think infrastructure that others depend on demands a measured, careful approach, and I try to live up to that whenever I can.

Practically speaking, whenever I use LLMs, I cannot help but tread slowly and carefully with them. I’ve found them to be invaluable at achieving a level of rigor that I could previously only dream about, but the fact that models don’t learn too much between sessions means they continue to make elementary mistakes. My work process makes me far slower in the moment than someone who one-shots software and moves on, but in the long run it lets me be done with a component, trusting that it works, and helps me build reliable systems out of well-designed parts. I hope that if you choose to use agents, this post inspires you to have a similar mindset.

From a systems design perspective, the release binaries are already arbitrary code, so curl | sh from the same origin doesn’t introduce a new trust boundary. One could reasonably critique the process of publishing release binaries at all. I think that on balance, publishing them in an auditable, transparent fashion is the best approach. ↩︎

Mukti is a Sanskrit, and later Hindi, word that means freedom or liberation. It has a spiritual meaning of release similar to moksha or nirvana, but also a more temporal meaning; e.g., FOSS is sometimes called mukt software in Hindi. ↩︎

My go-to is Claude Code’s bundled /simplify skill and the pr-review-toolkit plugin, though I also ask the agents to do an architectural/negative space review. ↩︎

As a result of this process, I also built an inventory of crates that were written by myself or Oxide, or that I otherwise trust — the LLMs are now instructed to use crates from this inventory when possible. They manage to follow it most of the time. ↩︎

#9959. Security incident disclosure — July 2026

Earlier this week, we detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure. This one was different from anything we had handled before in one important way: it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system - and we detected and dissected it largely with AI of our own.

We identified unauthorized access to a limited set of internal datasets and to several credentials used by our services. We are still completing our assessment of whether any partner or customer data was affected, and we will contact any affected parties directly as required. We have found no evidence of tampering with public, user-facing models, datasets, or Spaces, and our software supply chain (container images and published packages) was verified clean.

The intrusion started where AI platforms are uniquely exposed: the data-processing pipeline. A malicious dataset abused two code-execution paths in our dataset processing (a remote-code dataset loader and a template-injection in a dataset configuration) to run code on a processing worker. From there, the actor escalated to node-level access, harvested cloud and cluster credentials, and moved laterally into several internal clusters over a weekend.

The campaign was run by an autonomous agent framework (appearing to be built on an agentic security-research harness - used LLM still not known) executing many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes, with self-migrating command-and-control staged on public services. This matches the "agentic attacker" scenario the industry has been forecasting.

We are working with outside cybersecurity forensic specialists to investigate the issue and review our security policies and procedures. Finally, we have also reported this incident to law enforcement agencies.

As a precaution, we recommend rotating any access tokens and reviewing recent activity on your account. If you believe you are affected, or want to report a security concern, contact us at security@huggingface.co.

We are grateful to the teams across Hugging Face who responded around the clock, and we are sorry for any disruption this caused. Security is never finished; we will keep raising the bar.

The attack was initially surfaced through AI-assisted detection. Our anomaly-detection pipeline uses LLM-based triage over security telemetry to separate real signals from the daily noise, and it was the correlation of those signals that flagged the compromise.

To understand what a swarm of tens of thousands of automated actions did, we ran LLM-driven analysis agents over the full attacker action log, comprised of more than 17,000 recorded events. This allowed us to reconstruct the timeline, extract indicators of compromise, map the credentials touched, and separate genuine impact from decoy activity. Thanks to this approach, we were able to do in hours what would usually take days, and match the adversary's speed.

The choice of models we could use for this analysis was constrained in a way we did not anticipate; we describe this below.

When we started the log analysis, we first used frontier models behind commercial APIs. This did not work: the analysis requires submitting large volumes of real attack commands, exploit payloads, and C2 artifacts, and these requests were blocked by the providers' safety guardrails, which cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker. We ran the forensic analysis instead on zai-org/GLM-5.2, an open-weight model, on our own infrastructure. This had a second benefit: no attacker data, and none of the credentials it referenced, left our environment.

This experience points to a gap worth planning for. We do not know which model powered the attacker's agents, whether a jailbroken hosted model or an unrestricted open-weight one; either way, the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried. The practical lesson for defenders: have a capable model you can run on your own infrastructure vetted and ready before an incident, both to avoid guardrail lockout and to keep attacker data and credentials from leaving your environment. This is not an argument against safety measures on hosted models, and we are sharing this feedback with the providers concerned.

Autonomous, AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical. It lowers the cost of running a broad, patient, multi-stage campaign, and it operates at machine speed. Defending an online platform now means treating the data and model surface as a first-class attack surface, and using AI on defense to keep pace. We will keep investing there, and keep sharing what we learn.

#9957. Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker

Earlier this month I found a one-click universal XSS issue with uBlock Origin (the MV2 Firefox version, although a similar but less problematic issue also affected the MV3 version, uBO Lite), where a malicious website could trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters. Trusted filters can inject JavaScript code into pages, and so the malicious website could create a trusted filter on another website and run arbitrary JS in the context of any site. This issue is fixed now; you can read the GitHub advisory for some more details.

GPT-5.6 Sol did most of the hard work of finding the issue. I figured there might be some kind of UXSS from filter injection, so I asked it to take a look, and it found the issue. I then checked and verified the issue it proposed. I wrote all of the prose in this post myself; Claude wrote most of the code for the PoC.

uBlock Origin has an element picker that you can pull up by right-clicking on the page. You can use this to create a filter rule to block an element on the page without leaving the page.

The element picker is implemented by injecting an iframe to a URL like moz-extension://76b2331a-894c-4d25-8b89-fcce37e79cc4/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html. That page can talk to the extension background script and tell it to add filters.

On Firefox, the only information we needed to figure out was the extension internal UUID which is random per-installation.

On the default setup uBO has a lootdest.*##+js(no-fetch-if, adsbygoogle, war:googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js) filter rule (from uAssets), which hooks fetch. From inside the fetch hook, it makes an XHR request to moz-extension:///web_accessible_resources/googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js and returns the response from that as the fetch body, instead of actually making the request. The filter rule is intended to replace a network request for JS from an ad server with a dummy script that has the correct API but doesn’t do anything.

But the attacker website can itself hook the XHR made from inside the no-fetch-if hook to extract the random extension UUID.

Then the attacker website can run fetch('/adsbygoogle.js').catch(() => {}); to trigger the filter, and make their hooked XHR run. Note that there are several ways that the extension internal UUID could be leaked; it’s not just this one filter rule.

Then you can use that to iframe the element picker. Given an iframe element in the page, you just set its src to `moz-extension://${origin}/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html`.

Now we can drive the element picker. We can create a MessageChannel and do iframe.contentWindow.postMessage({ what: 'epickerStart' }, '*', [ch.port2]); to send it to the picker iframe. Then we talk to it: it sends us a start message, we send it a showDialog message with a filter and a resultsetDetails message1 to enable the create button and set opt.

Normally the picker restricts what filters you can enter, and doesn’t let you add scriptlet filters. But there’s a trick we can do to add arbitrary filters. There’s an opt field we set in the second message which is normally the type of network request to match (like image), and gets appended to the filter with a $ if set, like $image. But since we control it, we can put a newline in it and make it "image\ngoogle.com##+js(trusted-rpnt, script, ...)" to inject an arbitrary trusted filter that injects a script.2

This is where the main issue is - the element picker shouldn’t accept messages from the attacker. One of the fixes was having a secret password that the real element picker gets from the content script, that the element picker sends in the initial postMessage.

I didn’t bother actually implementing this, but malicious websites could overlay stuff on top of the embedded element picker or make it invisible by setting the iframe opacity to 0. So as long as the website can get the user to click on the page, it can add arbitrary trusted filters for arbitrary domains.

Filters added by the element picker are always treated as trusted (at least until a recompile), which is why it can add a trusted filter. If the user later changes their custom filters it would cause a recompile, clearing the filter trust. But in practice the attacker could just immediately open the victim webpage, so this doesn’t help much.

Originally I sent that message in reply to a dialogSetFilter message from the picker, but it turns out you can just send it right away instead of waiting to reply. ↩︎

Assuming the shown filter is a network filter. ↩︎
